translations.text: Therefore our hearts and bodies must be made ready to fight under the holy obedience of the commandments; and as for what our nature has less possible in us, let us ask the Lord
that he command the help of his grace to be given to us. And if, fleeing the punishments of hell, we wish to come to eternal life,
then while there is still time, and we are in this body, and there is time to fulfil all these things by this life of light,
we must now run and do what will profit us for eternity.
Therefore a school of the Lord's service must be established by us. In establishing it we hope to set down nothing harsh, nothing burdensome.

But if, as the reason of justice dictates, something a little stricter should come about for the correction of vices or the preservation of love, do not at once flee in terror from the way of salvation, which can only be begun with a narrow beginning. But as one progresses in the monastic life and in faith, with the heart enlarged, the way of God's commandments is run with the unspeakable sweetness of love,

so that, never departing from his teaching, persevering in his doctrine in the monastery until death, we may share by patience in the sufferings of Christ, so that we may also deserve to be sharers in his kingdom.
You who choose to put your neck under the gentle yoke of Christ, give your mind sweetly and willingly to the rule, that you may take honey.

Here is all the teaching of the old law and of the new; here is the divine order; here is the purest life. And the consecrated father composed the holy book. And these commandments he gave to be kept by his sons; and the minister of Christ, concealing [the authorship of] the master's work, brought it forth to all.
One reward awaits both, of both, in eternity. Listen, O son, to the commandments of the master!

And incline the ear of your heart, and willingly receive and effectively fulfil the admonition of the honourable father, so that through the labour of obedience you may return to him from whom you had gone away through the sloth of disobedience. To you, therefore, my word is now directed, whoever you are who, renouncing your own wills, take up the strongest and most glorious weapons of obedience to fight for the Lord Christ, the true king. First of all, whatever good thing you begin to do, ask him with most insistent prayer to bring it to completion,
so that he who has already deigned to count us in the number of his sons may not at any time be grieved by our evil deeds.
For at all times we must obey him with the good things he has given us, so that not only may he not, as an angry father, at any time disinherit his sons, but
also that he may not, as a dreaded lord provoked by our evils, hand over to eternal punishment, as the most wicked servants, those who would not follow him to glory. Let us therefore arise

at last, since Scripture rouses us and says: "It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep." And with our eyes opened to the divine light, let us hear with attentive ears what the divine voice, crying out daily, admonishes us, saying: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts." And again: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.
And what does he say?"
Come, sons, listen to me! I will teach you the fear of the Lord.

Run while you have the light of life, so that the darkness of death does not seize you! And the Lord, seeking his workman among the multitude of the people to whom he calls out these things, says again:
"Who is the man who wants life and longs to see good days?" If you hear this and answer, "I!",

God says to you: If you wish to have true and eternal life, keep your tongue from evil, and your lips so that they speak no deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. And when you have done these things, my eyes will be always upon you and my ears open to your prayers, and before you call on me, I will say to you: Behold, here I am. What can be sweeter to us than this voice of the Lord inviting us, dearest brothers?
See how the Lord in his loving-kindness shows us the way of life!

So let us gird our loins with faith, or with the keeping of good deeds, and with our feet shod in readiness for the gospel of peace, let us walk in his paths, so that we may be worthy to see him who calls us into his kingdom. If we wish to dwell in the house of that kingdom, we will not reach it unless we run there by good deeds. But let us ask the Lord with the prophet, saying to him:
Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest on your holy mountain?
After this question, brothers, let us hear the Lord answering and showing us the way to that same house, saying:

He who walks without stain and does what is right; who speaks truth in his heart; who has not practised deceit with his tongue; who has done no evil to his neighbour; who has not taken up a reproach against his neighbour;

who, when the accursed devil tries to persuade him of something, has driven him and his persuasion away from the sight of his heart, rejected him and brought him to nothing, and has taken hold of his small thoughts and dashed them against Christ. Those who fear the Lord do not grow proud of their good observance. Instead, they believe that the good that is in them cannot come from themselves but comes from the Lord.
They praise the Lord working in them, saying with the prophet: Not to us, Lord, but to your name give glory. Just as the apostle, too, did not ascribe anything of his preaching to himself, saying:
By the grace of God I am what I am. And again he himself says: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord.

That is why the Lord also said: Whoever hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man who built his house on rock. The floods came, the winds blew, and [?] struck that house.
And it [?] fell, because it was founded on rock.

Having said all this, the Lord waits for us each day to answer these holy admonitions of his with deeds. For this reason the days of this life are lengthened for us as a respite, so that we may make amends for our evils, as the apostle says: Or do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance? For indeed the merciful one says:
"I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn back and live."
So, brothers, when we asked the Lord about who shall dwell in his house, we heard the command given to the one who dwells there.
But if we fulfil the duty of the one who dwells there, we shall be heirs of the kingdom of heaven.
Of the kinds of monks. It is known that there are four kinds of monks. The first is that of the cenobites, that is, the monastic kind, fighting under a rule or an abbot (father).
Then the second kind is that of the anchorites, that is, the hermits (forest-dwellers): those who, not in the fresh fervour of a new life,

but through the long testing of the monastery, who have learned to fight against the devil with the help of many, and are now taught; and well trained in the brotherly battle-line for the single combat of the desert, they are now secure without the help of another, and with God helping are able to fight with a single hand or arm against the vices of the flesh or of the thoughts. The third, and truly the worst, kind of monks is that of the hypocrites [sarabaites], who have not been tested by any rule or by the experience of a master, as gold is by the furnace, but, softened like the nature of lead, still keeping faith with the world by their works, are known to lie to God by their tonsure. These, by twos or threes or indeed singly, without a shepherd, shut up not in the Lord's folds but in their own; for them the law is the pleasure of their desires. Whatever they think or choose,
that they call holy, and what they do not want, that they consider not permitted.

The fourth kind of monks is called that of the wanderers (gyrovagues). All their life long they go through various provinces and are lodged as guests in various cells for three or four days at a time. They are always wandering and never stable, serving their own wills and the unlawful enticements of the gullet, and in all things worse than the sarabaites.

Of the wretched way of life of all these it is better to be silent than to speak. Leaving these aside, then, let us come, with the Lord's help, to set in order the strongest kind, that of the cenobites.
He who is worthy to be over a monastery must always remember what he is called, and fulfil the name of the greater (superior) by his deeds.
For he is believed to act in the place of Christ in the monastery, since he is called by Christ's own name, as the apostle says:
"you have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry: Abba, Father."

And therefore he ought not to teach or establish or command anything outside the command of the Lord, far be it; but let his command or teaching be sprinkled, as the leaven of divine justice, in the minds of the disciples. Let him always be mindful that an examination will be made, in the fearful judgment of God, of both these matters: of his teaching and of the obedience of the disciples. And let him know that whatever lack of profit the father of the household can find in the sheep is laid to the fault of the shepherd.

So again it is that if all diligence has been given to an unquiet or disobedient flock of the shepherd, and all care has been applied to their diseased deeds, their shepherd, acquitted in the judgment of the Lord, may say to the Lord with the prophet: "I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have spoken your truth and your salvation.
But they, despising me, scorned me." And then at last, for the sheep disobedient to his care, let death itself be the punishment that prevails over them.

Therefore when anyone receives the name [of abbot], he ought to lead his disciples with a twofold teaching. That is, he should show all things good and holy by deeds more than by words: to understanding disciples he should set forth the commands of the Lord in words, but to the hard of heart and the simpler ones he should show the divine commands by his deeds. And whatever he teaches his disciples to be contrary, let him show by his deeds that it is not to be done, lest, while preaching to others, he himself be found reprobate, and lest at some time God say to him as he sins:
"Why do you declare my justice and take my covenant in your mouth?

"You indeed have hated my discipline and cast my words behind you." And: "You saw the straw in your brother's eye, and did not see the beam in your own." Let no distinction of persons be made by him in the monastery.

Let no one be loved more than another, except the one he finds better in good deeds or in obedience. Let a freeborn man not be placed ahead of one who comes to the service [of God] from servitude, unless there is some other reasonable cause.
But if, with justice dictating, it so

seems right, he may do that concerning the rank of anyone at all; otherwise, indeed, [let them keep] their own places. For whether slave or free, we are all one in Christ [literally "in the holy one"], and under one Lord we bear equally the warfare of service, for with God there is no partiality toward persons.
In this respect alone are we distinguished in his sight: if we are found better than others in good works and humble.
Indeed, let him show equal love to all, and let one discipline be applied to all, according to their deserts.
Indeed, in his teaching he must always keep the apostolic pattern, in which it says: "Reprove, entreat, rebuke!"
That is, mixing one time with another, gentleness with terrors, he should show the sternness of a master and the loving affection of a father.
That is: he must reprove the undisciplined and restless more harshly, but the obedient and gentle
[?] ... the patient, that they advance to better things, [let him] entreat.

We admonish him to rebuke and restrain the careless and the scornful. And let him not overlook the sins of those who do wrong, but as soon as they begin to arise, let him cut them off at the root as far as he is able, mindful of the danger of the priest of Shiloh. Those of more honorable and understanding mind he should indeed restrain with words at the first or second admonition, but the wicked, the hard, the proud, or the disobedient he should restrain with scourgings or bodily chastisement at the very beginning of the sin, knowing that it is written:
"The fool is not corrected by words," and again: "Strike your child with the rod, and you will free his soul from death."

He must always remember what he is, remember what he is called, and know that from the one to whom more is entrusted, more is required. And let him know how difficult and arduous a task he has taken on: to rule souls and to serve the characters of many, one indeed with gentle words, another with rebukes, another with persuasions. And according to the nature or understanding of each, let him so conform and adapt himself to all that he not only suffers no loss in the flock entrusted to him, but may indeed rejoice in the increase of the good flock. Above all, let him not, overlooking or holding in little regard the salvation of the souls entrusted to him,

take more concern for transitory, earthly, and perishable things, but let him always consider that he has taken on the ruling of souls, for which he will also have to give account. And let him not complain about perhaps having less property. Let him remember that it is written: "First seek the kingdom of God
and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you." And again:

"Nothing is lacking to those who fear him." And let him know that whoever has taken on the ruling of souls must prepare himself to give account on the day of judgment. And however great the number of brothers he knows he has under his care, let him recognize without doubt that on the day of judgment he will give account for all those same souls, and without doubt his own soul besides. And so, always fearing the shepherd's future examination concerning the sheep entrusted to him, while he guards against [having to give] account for others, he becomes more careful about his own; and while by his admonitions he supplies correction to others, he himself is corrected of his vices.
On calling the brothers to council.
Whenever any matters of the greatest importance are to be done in the monastery, let him call together

the whole community and himself say what is at issue. And hearing the counsel of the brothers, let him consider it within himself, and do what he judges more useful. We have said that all should be called to counsel for this reason: because the Lord often reveals to a younger person what is better. But let the brothers give counsel with all the submission of humility, so that they do not presume to defend boldly what has seemed right to them
but let it rather depend on the abbot's own judgment, so that whatever he judges to be more salutary, all obey him in it.
But just as it befits disciples to obey the master, so it befits him to arrange all things providently and justly.
In all things, then, let all follow the rule as master, and let no one turn away from it in anything.
Let no one in the monastery follow the will of his own heart, nor let anyone presume to contend insolently with his abbot, inside or outside the monastery.
If he does presume, let him be subject to the discipline of the rule.

The abbot himself, however, should do all things with the fear of God and in observance of the rule, knowing that he will without doubt have to give account of all his judgments to God, the most just judge. But if lesser matters are to be done in the monastery, let him use only the counsel of the seniors, as it is written: "Do all things with counsel, and afterwards you will not repent."
First, to love [?]. Then the neighbour as oneself!
Then: do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not covet, do not speak false witness; honour all men! What one does not want done to oneself, let him not do.

To deny oneself to oneself, in order to follow [?]. To chastise the body, not to embrace pleasures, to love fasting, to refresh the poor, to clothe the naked, to visit the sick, to bury the dead, to help in trouble, to console the grieving, to make oneself a stranger to the deeds of the world, nothing [?] love [?]
…to put before. Not to carry out anger, not to keep a time for wrath, not to hold grief in the heart, not to give a false peace, not to forsake love!
Not to swear, lest perhaps he perjure himself! To bring forth truth from the heart and the mouth, not to repay evil for evil, not to do injury, but to bear patiently what is done to him!
To love enemies! Not to curse back those who curse him, but rather to bless them!

To endure persecution for righteousness, not to be proud, not to be given to wine, not to be a glutton, not to be sleepy, not to be slothful, not to be a grumbler or a slanderer, to commit his hope to God!
When he sees some good in himself, let him attribute it to God, not to himself! But let him know that evil is always done by himself, and let him count it to himself!
To fear the day of judgment, to dread hell,

to long for eternal life with all spiritual desire, to keep death before his eyes daily as something to be feared, to guard the actions of his life at every hour, to know without doubt that God sees him in every place, to dash the evil thoughts that come into his heart against Christ at once and to reveal them to a spiritual elder, to keep his mouth from evil or perverse speech, not to love much talking, not to speak idle words or words fit for laughter, not to love much or boisterous laughter, to listen gladly to holy readings, to devote himself often to prayer, to confess daily to God in prayer, with tears or sighing, his past evils, to amend those same evils from then on, not to fulfil the desires of the flesh, to hate his own will, to obey the commands

in all things, even if he should act otherwise, which God forbid, mindful of the Lord's command: What they say, do; but what they do, choose not to do! Not to be called holy before he is, but first to be so, so that it may more truly be said!

To fulfil God's commandments in deeds every day; to love chastity; to hate no one; to have no jealousy or envy; not to love strife; to flee pride; to honor elders; to love the younger; to pray for enemies in the love of Christ; to return to peace with one who is at odds with you before the setting of the sun; and never to despair of God's mercy!

Behold, these are the teachings of the spiritual art. When we have carried them out day and night without ceasing and handed them back on the day of judgment, the Lord will repay us with the reward that he himself promised: "What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him." The workshops where we are to carry out all these things diligently are the enclosures of the monastery and stability in the community.

On obedience. The first step of humility is obedience without delay. This befits those who hold nothing dearer to themselves than Christ, whether because of the holy service that they have professed, or because of fear of hell, or for the glory of eternal life. As soon as anything has been commanded by a superior, as though it were commanded by God, they do not know how to allow delay in doing it. Of these the Lord says: "At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me."
Again he says to the teachers:
"He who hears you hears me." Truly, such as these at once leave what is theirs, abandoning their own will, at once with occupied hands

leave unfinished what they were doing, and with the near foot of obedience they follow the voice of the one commanding with deeds. And so, as if in a single moment, the master's command once spoken and the disciple's finished work are both carried out together quickly, in the swiftness of the fear of God,
by those who are pressed by the love of going to eternal life. Therefore they seize the narrow way, of which the Lord says:

"Narrow is the way that leads to life." So, not living by their own judgment, nor obeying their desires and wills, but walking by another's judgment and command, living in community, they desire [?] to be over them.

Without doubt such as these imitate the Lord's saying, in which he says: "I came not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me." But this same obedience is acceptable to God and sweet to men only

If something is commanded, and it is done not hesitantly, not [?] (lukewarmly?), not slowly, nor with murmuring or with the answer of one who is unwilling, then it is obedience, because the obedience that is given to superiors is given to God. For he himself said:

"Whoever hears you hears me." And it should be given by disciples with a good will, because [God] loves a cheerful giver. For if a disciple obeys with an ill will, and murmurs not only with his mouth but also in his heart, then even if he carries out the command, it is still not acceptable to God.
who sees his heart murmuring. For such a deed no grace follows; rather he incurs the punishment of murmurers, unless he makes amends with due satisfaction.
Let us do what the prophet said: "I said, I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue.
I have set a guard on my mouth.

I became mute and was humbled, and kept silent even from good things." Here the prophet shows that if we should sometimes refrain even from good words for the sake of silence, how much more should we stop from evil words because of the punishment for sin. So even perfect disciples, for the sake of the seriousness of silence, are seldom given permission to speak, even of good and holy and edifying things, because it is written:
"In much speaking you will not escape sin." And in another place it says: "Death and life are in the hands of the tongue."
Truly, it is fitting for the master to speak and teach; it is proper for the disciple to keep silent and listen.
Therefore, if anything has to be asked of superiors, let it be asked with the utmost reverence, so that one does not seem to speak more than is needful.
But jests, idle words, and words that stir up laughter we condemn everywhere and shut out forever. And we do not allow a disciple to open his mouth for such talk.

Holy Scripture cries out to us, saying: "Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted." When it says this, it shows us that every exaltation is a kind of pride. The prophet shows that he guards himself against this when he says:
"Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up, nor have I walked in great things, nor in wonders beyond me.
"If not humbly, but I exalted my soul, as a weaned child is upon its mother, so repay it upon my soul!"

Therefore, if we wish to reach the summit of the highest humility, and wish to come quickly to that heavenly exaltation to which one rises through the humility of the present life, then by our rising deeds that very ladder must be set up which appeared in a dream, on which descending
and ascending ones were shown to him.
Without doubt we understand that descent and ascent to mean nothing other than descending by exaltation and ascending by humility.
Truly, that upright ladder is our life in the world, which, once the heart is humbled, is raised up by the Lord to heaven.

We say that the side-poles of this ladder are our body and soul. Into these side-poles the divine calling has set various steps of humility, or of discipline, for those who are climbing. So the first step of humility is this: that a person always keeps the fear of God before his eyes and flees forgetfulness altogether, and always remembers everything that God has commanded, how those who despise [... the text breaks off]

[...those who despise] God [will be] burned in hell for their sins, and likewise let him always turn over in his mind the eternal life that is prepared for those who fear God. And keeping himself at every hour from sin and vice, that is, of the thoughts, the tongue, the eyes, the hands, the feet, or his own will, but also hastening to cut off the desires of the flesh, let a man consider that he is always seen from heaven by God at every hour, and that his deeds are seen in every place by the sight of the Godhead and are reported at every hour. The prophet shows us this when he shows God to be always present in our thoughts, saying:
"God searching hearts and reins," and again:

"The Lord knows the thoughts of men," and again he says: "You have understood my thoughts from afar," and "the thought of man will confess to you." Indeed, so that he may be careful about his perverse thoughts, let the useful brother always say
in his heart:
"Then I shall be spotless before him, if I keep myself from my iniquity."
Truly, we are forbidden to do our own will, since Scripture says to us: "And turn away from your own wills."
Again, we ask God in prayer that his will be done in us. Truly, then, we are rightly taught not to do our own will, when we beware of what Holy Scripture says:
"There are ways which are thought right by men, whose end sinks down to the depth of hell."

And then when we beware of what is said of the negligent: "They are corrupt and have become loathsome in their desires." Indeed, in the desires of the flesh let us believe that God is always present to us, since the prophet says to the Lord: "Before you is all my desire." Evil desire must therefore be guarded against, because death is set beside the entrance of pleasure. Therefore Scripture commands, saying:

"Do not go after your desires." Indeed, if the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the evil, [and he] always looks down from heaven on the children of men to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God,
and if our works are reported daily, by day and by night, to the Lord our maker by the angels assigned to us, then one must truly be on guard at every hour,

[then] as the prophet says in the psalm, [let us beware] lest God at any hour see us turning aside to evil and become useless. And though he spares us in this time, because he is merciful and waits for us daily to turn to the better, [let us beware] lest he say to us in the future:

"These things you did, and I kept silent." The second step of humility is if someone, not loving his own will, does not delight in fulfilling his desires, but imitates in his deeds that voice of the one saying:
"I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me." Again Scripture says:

"Will brings punishment, and necessity wins a crown." The third step of humility is that someone, for the love of God, submits himself in all obedience to his superior, imitating the Lord, of whom the apostle says: "Becoming obedient to the Father unto death."

The fourth [step] is if, in that same obedience, in hard and adverse things, or likewise in whatever injuries are inflicted, he embraces [?] with a silent conscience and, enduring, does not grow weary or give way, as Scripture says: "He who perseveres to the end, he shall be saved." Likewise:

"Let your heart be strengthened, and endure." And showing that the faithful man must endure all things for the Lord, even adverse things, he says in the person of those who suffer: "For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for the slaughter."
And secure in the hope of the divine reward, they follow on, rejoicing and saying: "But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us." Likewise in another place:
"You have tested us; you have tried us with fire, as silver is tried with fire."
You led us into the snare; you laid hardship upon our back."

…so as to show that we ought to be under a superior, it follows: "You have set men over our heads." And also the commandment [of the Lord] in adversities and in injuries [?]: those struck on the cheek offer also the other; to one who takes away the tunic they let go the cloak as well; compelled to go one mile, they go two,
and with Paul the apostle they endure false brothers,

and they endure persecution, and they bless those who speak evil of them. The fifth [?] is if he does not hide from his [?], through humble confession, all the evil thoughts that come into his heart, or the evils he has done in secret. Scripture urges us to this, saying: "Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him." Again:
"Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever." Again:
"I have made my transgression known to you; my injustices I [?] covered.
I said: I will declare my injustice against myself, Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin." The sixth, if a monk, content with every meanness and utmost lowliness,

in all the things that are laid on him, he judges himself a bad and unworthy workman, saying to himself with the prophet: "I have been brought to nothing and I did not know it; I have become like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you."

The seventh [?] is if he not only declares with his tongue that he is lower and more contemptible than all, but also believes it in the inmost love [?] of his heart, humbling himself and saying with the prophet: "But I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and an outcast of the people."
"Exalted, humbled, confounded." Again: "It is good for me that you have humbled me, so that I may learn your commandments!"

The eighth, if he does nothing except what the common rule of the monastery or the examples of the elders urge. If he keeps his tongue from speaking and, keeping silence, does not speak until he is asked, as Scripture says, that "in much speaking sin is not escaped" and that "a talkative man is not set straight upon the earth."
The tenth, if he is not easy and quick to laughter, for it is written: "The fool raises his voice in laughter." He speaks gently,
without laughter, humbly, with seriousness; he speaks few and reasonable words, and is not loud of voice, as it is written:
"The wise man is known by few words." The twelfth, if he always shows humility not only in his heart but also in his very body to those who see him, that is, in work,
in the garden,

on the road, in the field, or wherever he is, sitting, walking or standing, with his head always bowed and his eyes fixed on the ground; at every hour he considers himself guilty of his sins and thinks himself already brought before the dreadful judgment, always saying in his heart what the publican of the Gospel said with his eyes fixed on the ground: "I, a sinner, am not worthy to lift my eyes to heaven"; and again with the prophet: "I am bowed down and humbled on every side."
"So, when all these steps of humility have been climbed,

[the monk] will soon come to the love of God that, being perfect, casts out fear. Through this love he begins to keep everything that before he did not observe without fear. He keeps it without any labor, as if by nature, from habit. He keeps it no longer out of fear of hell, but out of love [?] and out of that good habit itself and delight in the virtues. These the Lord has deigned to show by the Holy Spirit in his workman, made clean from vices [and] sins.

In wintertime, according to the consideration of reason, one is to rise at the eighth hour of the night, so that one rests a little beyond midnight and rises likewise having digested. What remains after the vigils is to be used by those brothers who need some part of the psalter
or of the readings, for study. From
however,

to the time mentioned above, let the time be arranged so that the vigils are done with a very short interval, in which the brothers go out for the needs of nature. Immediately afterwards the morning lauds, which are to be done as the light begins, follow.
written above, first the verse; in the second [?] it is to be said: "will proclaim"
To which the third psalm is to be added
After this, the ninety-fourth psalm: with an antiphon, or at any rate to be sung.

After this let six psalms follow. When these have been said and the verse has been said, let [?] bless, and with all sitting on the benches, let three readings be [?] in turn by the brothers from the book on the lectern, between which three

After the third [psalm], the one who sings is to say the Glory. When the singer begins to say it, all are to rise at once from their seats in honor and reverence of the Holy Trinity. Books are to be read at the vigils, both of the Old Testament and of the New, of divine authority, and also their explanations, which were made by well-known orthodox fathers.
After these three lessons with their responsories, let the other six psalms follow, to be sung.
After these, let the lesson of the Apostle follow, to be recited from memory, and the humble prayer "Lord, have mercy on us." Thus let the vigils of the night be ended.
In all of them, as was said above, let the quantity of psalm-singing be kept, except
that the lessons from the book are not to be read at all, because of the shortness of the nights.
But instead of the three lessons, one from the Old Testament is to be read [?] from memory, followed by a short [?]. All the rest is to be done as has been said.
That is, never less than the number of twelve psalms is to be said at the vigils, except the third [?]
and the ninety-fourth psalm.
